ENTER THE ECONOMIC DEPRESSION

Gross Domestic Profit dropped by 10% between the 3rd quarter of 2007 and 3rd quarter of 2010. The stage was set. Legitimate reasons for social unrest, doubt towards the governing body and the questioning of how it happened and how appropriately it was handled.

As an Icelandic citizen, the time leading up to the crash, you'd have never guessed the looming crash. Their government assured the people that things were fine and the status quo was being maintained. However, by October 2008, a country with a historically low unemployment rate had reach an unemployment rate of 18%. This force focused a then narrow view of financial responsibility and governmental procedures into a panoramic view of the economic and political landscape. Not the world being displayed for them. Upon the assessment of their government and it's handling of their socioeconomic situation, only one course was viable: revolution. It began one Saturday in mid-October. Hodur Torfuson, a singer/songwriter, took to a public square in Reykjavik with an open microphone and asked random passing citizens to speak. The following Saturday was the first formally organized protest. Initially dominated by one speaker with one view on how to fix their predicament. One view, or plan, on how to reform their misshapen country wouldn't suffice. Revolution must represent many people with varying ideologies, equally through mutual sacrifice for the betterment of society. On the third Saturday, with a relatively fast incubation, they organized their campaign and formed the power which led Iceland to reformation through revolution.

VOICES OF THE PEOPLE

Raddir Folksins was formed by the people and to ensure a stable, prosperous future for the people. It's goal lofty and fight hard, but the Voices of the People would not be silenced. In order to move their agenda along, a streamlined set of demands were crafted in order to define the change the people deemed a necessity.

1. The Resignation of the Government.

2. The Resignation of the Central Banks Board.

3. The Resignation of the Financial Security Authority's Board

4. New Elections Held As Soon As Possible.

Each Saturday the Raddir Folksins gathered and protested the obvious failures of their then elected leadership. Their goals clear, they wouldn't rest till changes were made. From October through December, the Revolution gained momentum. Finally, on the last day of December, at a hotel in Reykjavik were found the Icelandic media and it's politicians. The media interviewing the politicians and recalling the past year. Hopes high for the New Year. The media initiated the conversation of all the financial accomplishments that were made that year. Having 3 banks fail, astoundingly high unemployment, the crashing of their currency and a freezing of foreign financial transactions had left a bitter taste of the Raddir Folksins' mouths. They wouldn't suffer the lies that any positive accomplishments were made. With their pots and pans and all things clanging mental, the Revolution attempted to drown out the broadcast. Unhindered, the politician and his media lackey continued. Enraged, the Raddir Folksins took the step all revolutions must come to naturally: action.

They scaled the fences; no walls, laws or lies were going to stop them in their determinations of thwarting the media and their play.The protestors took the media cables and severed them, totally disrupting the broadcast. To ensure the show mustn't go on, the proceeded to burn the cables. Thus began the Kitchenware Revolution and the New Year.

From this point things moved more quickly and decisively. On January 20th, 2009, the Raddir Folksins had some 2,000 protestors gathered at the Althingi House (Parliament). Pots and pans and all things that clang in hand, disorder and disruption were the goal. Noise gave way to action as rocks, eggs and Icelandic yogurt were hurled at the building. Shattering windows and staining the building.

Citizens were pepper sprayed and arrested. Over 30 people incarcerated before the days end. The people had been patient long enough. Crowds stayed at the Althingi House all night. Making bonfires from whatever could be found and burned. They were there to stay and they wanted everyone to know that this social unrest was their way of communicating to Those With Power that their power was waning. Soon to be non-existent. The 21st of January the Revolution surrounded the Prime Ministers car, acting with total intent on absolute disruption, they took to taking red paint and throwing entire gallons on the government buildings. The night of the 22nd tensions between the Revolution and the government hit their highest point to date. A fever swept through them, instigating the boiling point which would lead the police to use tear gas on its own citizens for the first time in sixty years. The Revolutionaries had taken to throwing rocks at any glass in range. Into the Althingi House went stone after stone. Striking and injuring police officers located within.

All week, day and night, the Revolution rolled on. At its height, approximately 10,000 Icelanders filled the streets. On the 23rd of January, Prime Minister Haarde announcced that there would be elections held in May. Elections he would most certainly abstain from. He then resigned himself and his cabinet. The next day, the Minister of Commerce Bjorn Sigurdsson resigned as did the Director of the Financial Supervisory Board and it's members.

THREE OUT OF FOUR DEMANDS MET

The Revolution bent the government to its will. Three-quarters of its demands having been met, the people were in a state of elation. However, the Central Bank Director and its board remained untouched. An interim government was formed and the Raddir Folksins ceased their Saturday demonstrations for the first time since it began, some three months prior. The reprieve was short, having only one Saturday without protest. They resumed their duties on February 8th on the steps of Parliament they demanded that the three governing officials of the Central Bank be fired. The officials refused. A last gasp of tyranny holding tight to whatever power remained. The acting Prime Minister Sigurdardottir publicly expressed disappointment in the three officials insistence on retaining their positions.

If they wouldn't leave, the Revolution wouldn't allow them to work. On February 9th the Raddir Folksins created a blockade to keep the remaining officials from entering Parliament. Chief Official Fridriksson resigned. One down, two to go.

The Revolution at full steam ahead, protests continued throughout February. During this time the Interim Government crafted the Central Banking Law Reform. Amendments to the Central Banking Act abolished the need for three governing officials and instituted the ruling of the Central Bank by one director and a deputy. The writing was on the wall. Change had been demanded and changes were being made.

The Voices of The People wouldn't relent. Their cause just and their actions warranted. The law reforms became inevitability. The remaining two officials stepped down on February 26th. The following day the Central Banking Amendments passed. The Raddir Folksins had made demands which were needed in order to pave a way out from under irresponsible rulers. They stood together in the face of all the powers reigned, unwavering in their resolve they pushed back to reclaim what was theirs. The people prevailed.
